parts.article:
The Art of Deception
 
Do tiny changes of facial expression show whether someone is telling lies?
 
(A) Forty years ago, the research psychologist Dr Paul Ekman was addressing a group of young psychiatrists in training when he was asked a question, the answer to which has kept him busy ever since. Suppose the group wanted to know whether a particular patient who swears they are telling the truth really is. They look and sound sincere. So here is the question: is there any way you can be sure they are telling the truth? Ekman did not know the answer then, but he wanted to find out.
 
(B) As part of his research, he had already filmed a series of 12-minute interviews with psychiatric patients. In a subsequent conversation, one of the patients told him that she had lied to him. So Ekman sat and looked at the film but saw nothing noteworthy. Then he slowed it down and looked again. Then he slowed it down even further. And suddenly, there, across just two frames of the film, he saw it: an intense expression of extreme anguish. It lasted less than a fifteenth of a second, but once he had spotted the first expression, he soon found three more examples in that same interview. He termed his discovery “micro-expressions”: very rapid, intense demonstrations of emotion that the subject intended to conceal.
 
(C) Over the course of the next four decades, Ekman successfully demonstrated a proposition first suggested by Charles Darwin: that the ways in which we express rage, disgust, contempt, fear, surprise, happiness and sadness are universal. The facial muscles triggered by those seven basic emotions are, he has shown, essentially standard, regardless of language and culture, from the US to Japan and Brazil to Papua New Guinea. What is more, expressions of emotion are impossible to suppress and, particularly when we are lying, micro-expressions of powerfully felt emotions will inevitably flit across our face before we get the chance to stop them.
 
(D) Fortunately for liars, most people will fail to spot these fleeting signals of inner torment. Of the 15 000 Ekman has tested, only 50 people, whom he calls “naturals”, have been able to do it. But given a little more training, Ekman says, almost anyone can develop the skill. He should know: since these tests were completed in the mid-1980s and the first publication of his research, he has been called in by the FBI and CIA (among countless more law enforcement and other agencies around the world), not just to solve cases, but to teach them how to use his technique for themselves. He has held workshops for defence and prosecution lawyers, health professionals, even jealous spouses, all of them wanting to know exactly when someone is not being 100 percent candid.
 
(E) Most recently, Ekman's research has resulted in a new television series about the exploits of the fictional Dr Cal Lightman, a scientist who studies involuntary body language to discover not only if you are lying, but why you might have been motivated to do so. According to the publicity blurb, Lightman is a human lie detector, even more accurate than a polygraph test. Ekman concedes he was sceptical when the producer first approached him with the idea of turning his life's work into a TV series, and initially would have stopped the project if he could. In particular, he was fearful that the show would exaggerate the effectiveness of his techniques and create the quite inaccurate impression among audiences that criminals could no longer hope to get away with lying. In the worst-case scenario, he was concerned about unfair convictions—that one day someone not properly trained in his techniques might be sitting on a jury and wrongly find someone guilty of a crime simply on the basis of a television programme.
 
(F) In the end, though, he was won over because the series is unusual in several respects. It is the first time, as far as Ekman is aware, that a commercial TV drama has been based on the work of just one scientist. That scientist is also deeply involved in the project, talking through plot ideas and checking five successive drafts of each script to ensure details are correct. He was also impressed with the producer's manifestly serious and well-intentioned reasons for making the programme. Now that the first series has been completed, he believes probably 80–90 per cent of the show is based on fact and that's good enough for what it is. After all, it is a drama, not a documentary.
 
(G) Ekman, incidentally, professes to have been a terrible liar ever since he was a small boy and observes that the ability to detect a lie and the ability to lie successfully are completely unrelated. He has been asked by people running for high office if he could teach them to become more credible with the public but has always refused to use his skills in that way on ethical grounds. He also insists that there are various kinds of lies. A “true” lie can be identified by having two essential characteristics: there must be a deliberate intent to mislead and there must be no notification that this is what is occurring. This means that an actor or a poker player isn't a true liar. They are supposed to deceive you—it's part of the game—and the same is true of flattery. He prefers to focus on the kinds of lies where the liar would be in grave trouble if they were found out, and where the target would feel properly aggrieved if they knew.
parts.questions:
Questions 27 – 31
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 27 – 31 on your answer sheet.

Q27 According to the writer, Ekman became interested in lying after a question from his

  • A peers
  • B patients
  • C students
  • D teachers

Q28 The writer refers to the 12-minute interviews in order to

  • A illustrate how frequently patients lie
  • B describe the origins of Ekman's theories
  • C compare Ekman's research to previous studies
  • D show how patients' behaviour is affected by filming

Q29 What is the writer's point in the third paragraph?

  • A Micro-expressions are common to all people.
  • B Recent research has refuted an old idea.
  • C With practice we can learn to control our micro-expressions.
  • D Human society is too complex to allow for generalisations.

Q30 What are we told about Ekman's conclusions from his tests?

  • A It's natural for people to lie.
  • B Few untrained people can detect lying.
  • C Most liars suffer from periods of depression.
  • D All of his subjects were trained to identify micro-expressions.

Q31 What point does the writer make about Ekman's techniques in the fourth paragraph?

  • A They take a decade to teach.
  • B They have been in great demand.
  • C They have aroused the suspicions of some agencies.
  • D They can be used by a limited range of occupations.

Write the correct letter, A-I, in boxes 32 – 36 on your answer sheet.

Ultimately, though, he has given the show his blessing because he is not aware of any other comparable programme based on a single person's .   • A consequences

Questions 37 – 40
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 37 – 40 on your answer sheet, write.

Q37 Ekman regrets the lies he told as a child.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q38 People who are good at lying tend to be good at detecting lies.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q39 Ekman has worked with poker players to help them lie more convincingly.

  • A YES
  • B NO

  • A YES

reference:
Q27

干扰 不要被“psychiatrists（精神科医师）”误导去选 B（病人），“in training”表明他们是正在学习的学生身份。

句子 (Paragraph A) "...Ekman was addressing a group of young psychiatrists in training when he was asked a question..."

解析 A段提到Ekman当时正在给一群“受训中的年轻精神科医师（young psychiatrists in training）”讲话，并被其中一人提问，这些人本质上是他的学生，对应选项 C (students)。

Q28

解析 B段描述了Ekman如何重看这12分钟的采访录像，通过慢放发现了“微表情”，从而引出了他的理论基础，对应选项 B（描述Ekman理论的起源）。

干扰 这段文字不仅是描述采访本身，重点在于通过采访录像发现了（discovery）微表情，这是理论的源头。

句子 (Paragraph B) "...he saw it: an intense expression of extreme anguish... He termed his discovery “micro-expressions”..."

Q29

解析 C段指出Ekman成功论证了无论语言和文化如何（regardless of language and culture），我们表达情绪的方式是通用的（universal），微表情也是如此，对应选项 A（微表情对所有人都是共同的）。

干扰 B选项（反驳旧观点）错误，原文是说证实了达尔文的提议；C选项（学会控制）错误，原文说微表情是“impossible to suppress（无法抑制的）”。

句子 (Paragraph C) "...demonstrated a proposition... that the ways in which we express rage... are universal... expressions of emotion are impossible to suppress..."

Q30

句子 (Paragraph D) "Of the 15 000 Ekman has tested, only 50 people... have been able to do it."

解析 D段提到在他测试的15,000人中，只有50人（naturals）能做到识别谎言，说明极少数未经训练的人能检测出谎言，对应选项 B。

干扰 原文说“most people will fail to spot... only 50 people... have been able to do it”，这与B选项“Few untrained people can detect lying”完全一致。

Q31

解析 D段后半部分列举了FBI、CIA、律师、健康专家甚至嫉妒的配偶都来找他学习技术，说明需求量巨大，对应选项 B（需求很大）。

干扰 D选项（限于有限的职业）错误，原文列举了多种多样的群体（lawyers, health professionals, spouses...），范围很广。

句子 (Paragraph D) "...he has been called in by the FBI and CIA (among countless more...)... He has held workshops for defence and prosecution lawyers, health professionals, even jealous spouses..."

Q32

解析 题目说Ekman担心会助长观众的____，原文E段提到他担心节目会夸大效果并在观众中造成“inaccurate impression（不准确的印象）”，即错误的观念，对应选项 C (false beliefs)。

干扰 “Inaccurate impression” 就是 “false beliefs” 的同义替换。

句子 (Paragraph E) "...feared that the show would... create the quite inaccurate impression among audiences..."

Q33

解析 题目说他担心节目会导致____无法实施，原文E段提到他担心“unfair convictions（不公正的定罪）”，即某人可能被错误定罪，这意味着正义（justice）未得到伸张，对应选项 E。

干扰 “Unfair convictions” 和 “wrongly find someone guilty” 都是对 “justice not being carried out” 的具体描述。

句子 (Paragraph E) "...concerned about unfair convictions—that one day someone... might wrongly find someone guilty..."

Q34

干扰 “Work of a scientist” 在语境下即指代他的“research”。

句子 (Paragraph F) "...a commercial TV drama has been based on the work of just one scientist."

解析 题目说这是基于单一个人的____，原文F段提到这是第一次有商业电视剧基于“work of just one scientist（仅一位科学家的工作）”，这里的work指的就是他的研究，对应选项 H。

Q35

解析 题目说制片人的____是另一个惊喜，原文F段提到Ekman对制片人制作节目的“manifestly serious and well-intentioned reasons（显而易见严肃且善意的理由）”印象深刻，理由即动机，对应选项 D。

干扰 “Reasons for making the programme” 就是 “motives”。

句子 (Paragraph F) "He was also impressed with the producer's manifestly serious and well-intentioned reasons for making the programme."

Q36

解析 题目说Ekman对节目的整体____感到满意，原文F段提到他认为节目“80–90 per cent... is based on fact（基于事实）”，这对他来说足够好了，即准确性，对应选项 F。

干扰 “Based on fact” 对应 “accuracy”。

句子 (Paragraph F) "...he believes probably 80–90 per cent of the show is based on fact and that's good enough..."

Q37

句子 (Paragraph G) "Ekman, incidentally, professes to have been a terrible liar ever since he was a small boy..."

解析 G段只提到Ekman自称从小就是个“糟糕的撒谎者（terrible liar）”，但并未提及他是否对此感到“后悔（regrets）”，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 “Terrible liar”指撒谎技术差，不等于“后悔撒谎”。

Q38

解析 题目说擅长撒谎的人也擅长识破谎言。原文G段明确说“detect a lie（识破谎言）”和“lie successfully（成功撒谎）”的能力是“completely unrelated（完全不相关的）”，相互矛盾，选 NO。

干扰 “Completely unrelated” 直接否定了题目中的关联性（tend to be）。

句子 (Paragraph G) "...observes that the ability to detect a lie and the ability to lie successfully are completely unrelated."

Q39

解析 G段提到“演员或扑克玩家（actor or poker player）”不是真正的骗子，但并未提及Ekman是否曾与扑克玩家“合作（worked with）”帮助他们，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 文中只是拿扑克玩家举例说明什么是“非真正的谎言”，没有提到任何合作关系。

句子 (Paragraph G) "This means that an actor or a poker player isn't a true liar."

Q40

解析 题目说他更关注那些有严重后果的谎言。原文G段最后一句说他更喜欢关注那种“撒谎者如果被发现会有大麻烦（grave trouble）”的谎言，选 YES。

干扰 “Grave trouble” 对应 “serious consequences”。

句子 (Paragraph G) "He prefers to focus on the kinds of lies where the liar would be in grave trouble if they were found out..."
